questions.question: Name the three parts of every building cost and explain what each depends on, and state the two allowances a realistic estimate adds.
questions.expected_answer: Materials, which depend on the design and the quantities it needs; labour, which depends on the skill of the workers and the number of days the job takes; and transport, which depends on distance from suppliers and the number of trips. A realistic estimate adds about 10 percent to materials for waste and breakages and about 10 percent to the total as a contingency for the unexpected, such as weather, buried services or price rises.

questions.question: A ramp is 7 200 millimetres long, 1 200 wide and averages 300 thick. Calculate the concrete volume and the approximate cement, sand and stone needed if mixed on site.
questions.expected_answer: Volume is 7.2 times 1.2 times 0.3, which is about 2.6 cubic metres. A cubic metre of site-mixed concrete for paths and ramps needs about 7 bags of cement, 0.5 cubic metres of sand and 0.5 cubic metres of stone, so 2.6 cubic metres needs about 18 bags of cement, 1.3 cubic metres of sand and 1.3 cubic metres of stone, plus about 10 percent for waste.

questions.question: Describe the layout of a cost estimate for the stairs and ramp and explain why every figure must be traceable.
questions.expected_answer: A table with columns for item, quantity, unit, unit price and total, in three sections: materials such as cement, sand, stone, mesh, rail tube, bolts and shuttering with 10 percent waste; labour as workers times days at local daily rates; and transport as deliveries or bakkie trips. Subtotal, then add 10 percent contingency. Every figure must be a quantity measured from the drawing times a price from a named supplier on a stated date, so that the tender board can check any line and the estimate can be updated when prices change.
